en: The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai explains the second chapter, "Extensive Explanation of the [Buddha’s] Life Span," within the context of the six meanings. Among these, there is no section on the rarity of the Dharma;
first, he reveals the provisional, next, he manifests the real; third, he cites the five turbidities to explain the skillful means; fourth, he discriminates against the false.
"Thickly trusting in the one reality, the five are without falsehood.
"I am now also like this": I am Śākyamuni; having first manifested three and subsequently one, I am no different from the four Buddhas, and thus it is said, "I am also like this."
"Knowing that sentient beings have various desires" refers to the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of the five vehicles.
Those of the past are called "faculties" (indriya), those of the present are called "desires" (chanda), and those of the future are called "dispositions" (gotra).
"Deep-seated attachment" refers to the faculties (*indriya*).
"Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the provisional teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) established according to what is appropriate for beings.
The phrase "all of this is for the sake of attaining the Single Buddha Vehicle" reveals the reality [of the teaching].
The Buddha Vehicle is the oneness of the teaching; "all" is the oneness of practice; and that which is known by the knowledge of all modes is the oneness of principle.

Regarding the passage, "In the ten directions there are not even two vehicles, let alone three," this is the third section, which explains the disclosure of the provisional by citing the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*).

Before citing the five turbidities, its underlying intent is first indicated: previously it was explained that the Buddhas disclose the provisional to reveal the real; however, it has not yet been clarified how they conceal the real to establish the provisional. That Dharma is pure, tranquil, and uniform like space; therein, there is not even the provisional of "carrying two" or "carrying three," much less the provisional of "single three" or "single five."

It is precisely because the obstacles of the five turbidities are so heavy that [the truth] cannot actually be proclaimed; thus, one must employ the provisional means of the "single five" and "single three," as well as the provisional means of the "conjoined two" and "conjoined three. Therefore, it is said: "Within the One Buddha Vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three. This "distinguishing and teaching of three" refers to the three that are either conjoined with two or conjoined with three, as well as the three that are the "single five" and "single three."
Regarding the "five turbidities" (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), there are four distinct sections:
first, the enumeration; second, the listing of names; third, their essential characteristics; and fourth, the explanation and conclusion.
The enumeration and listing of names are as in the text.
The term "thus" (*evam*) clarifies the essential nature and characteristics [of the kalpa-turbidity].

The turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) has no separate substance; a kalpa is a long duration, while a kṣaṇa is a short duration. It is merely in reference to the four turbidities that this provisional name is established. As the text says, "at the time of the confusion of the kalpa-turbidity," this is precisely that meaning.

The defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) likewise has no separate essence; it is a provisional designation established upon the basis of views, pride, and karmic retribution. As the text states, "the impurities of sentient beings are heavy," this refers precisely to that meaning.

The defilement of afflictions (kleśa-kaṣāya) takes the five dull fetters as its essence; the defilement of views (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya) takes the five sharp fetters as its essence; and the defilement of lifespan (āyuḥ-kaṣāya) takes the continuity of matter and mind as its essence, and so forth.

As for these signs: during this time, the four turbidities intensify and converge. When hatred intensifies, weapons and warfare arise; when greed intensifies, famine arises; and when delusion intensifies, epidemics arise. Because these three calamities arise, afflictions double in prevalence and various views burn even more fiercely. Physical forms and mental states become coarse and debased, and one receives evil reputations and foul appellations. Years are crushed and lifespans diminished as the various turbidities converge, like turbulent waters rushing toward darkness where wind and waves surge and fish and dragons churn about; there is not a single thing to rely upon, for it is the power of time that causes all this.

It is like when, at the beginning of a kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven fall to earth and the earth causes them to develop desire; or like when the Trāyastriṃśa gods enter the Rough and Astringent Garden (Kharasvaka-udyāna) and the garden gives rise to thoughts of strife—this is called the characteristic of the kalpa-turbidity (kalpa-kaṣāya).

Regarding the turbidity of afflictions: the ocean of greed receives all streams yet is never satiated; the venomous serpent of anger inhales poison and agitates the world; the darkness of ignorance is more stubborn and dull than lacquer or ink; pride looks down upon others with haughty disregard without measure; and the net of doubt lacks faith such that the truth cannot be told—these are the characteristics of the turbidity of afflictions.

Regarding the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): where there is no person, one says there is a person; where there is the Path, one says there is no Path. The sixteen types of speculative views, the sixty-two [views], and so forth, are like a net and resemble a dense forest; they entangle and distort one so that one cannot escape—this is the characteristic of the turbidity of views.

Regarding the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): they grasp at form and mind to establish a single sovereign self. Like sticky glue to which nothing fails to adhere, they wander through the six realms of existence, taking birth everywhere—whether as poor or short-lived, or as long-lived or wealthy. This is the characteristic mark of the turbidity of sentient beings.

Regarding the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣkaṣāya*): born in the morning, one perishes by evening; appearing by day, one vanishes by night. Like shifting waves or swirling smoke, it does not abide for even a moment; such is the characteristic of the turbidity of lifespan.
The characteristics of turbidity are manifold and cannot be fully described.

As for the sequence: afflictions and views constitute the root; from these two turbidities, sentient beings come into being; from sentient beings, there arises the maintenance of life; when these four pass through time, it is called the *kalpa-turba* (the age of turbulence).
Regarding the investigation:

Question—If the five turbidities constitute an obstacle to the Great [Vehicle], why is it that in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* there are those who hear the Dharma without having yet eliminated these turbidities?
Answer:
This should be analyzed through four permutations:

first, those with sharp faculties in the Mahāyāna but heavy obstacles; because their faculties are sharp, the heavy obstacles cannot obstruct them—this refers to those who first hear the Mahāyāna in this land, such as those for whom the *Avataṃsaka* was taught;
second, those with sharp faculties and light obstacles.
Third, those with dull faculties but light hindrances who hear the Mahāyāna in the pure lands of other directions;
fourth, those with dull faculties and heavy hindrances, such as the class of Śāriputra in this land, who must first remove their turbidity before they can hear the Mahāyāna.
Question:
Do the five turbidities obstruct the Small [Vehicle]?
Answer:
This is discussed from the perspective of the Hīnayāna and should be analyzed through four permutations:
those with sharp faculties who have abandoned light hindrances, yet their obstacles cannot obstruct them, such as Śāriputra;
and those with sharp faculties who have abandoned heavy hindrances, yet their obstacles likewise cannot obstruct them, such as Aṅgulimāla.
Those with dull faculties who possess light hindrances do not encounter obstacles; Pāṇṭaka is an example of this.
Those with dull faculties who possess heavy hindrances do indeed encounter obstacles; such individuals do not hear the Hīnayāna and do not attain liberation.
Question:
Why is it that there are those who hear the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings even though they do not belong to the *Avataṃsaka* nor to the Tripiṭaka?
Answer:
Regarding these four teachings, each teaching is analyzed through four gates.
Those with sharp faculties who are hindered by light [afflictions] enter by hearing the gate of "neither empty nor existent.
Those with sharp faculties who are hindered by heavy [afflictions] enter by hearing the gate of "both empty and existent."
Regarding those of dull faculties who are hindered by the light [afflictions], they enter through hearing the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
regarding those of dull faculties who are hindered by the heavy [afflictions], they enter through hearing the gate of existence (*bhava*).

The four gates of the two teachings are distinguished according to the Hīnayāna; the four gates of the two teachings are distinguished according to the Mahāyāna. These points can be understood through careful analysis, and so forth.
Question:
Regarding the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), why do they generally obstruct the Great [Vehicle] but not the Small?
Answer:

The defilement of sentient beings is heavy; they falsely reckon the five aggregates to possess the four virtues. If they hear of "permanence" and "self," they immediately cling to what is not as being so. Like an old physician who is dull-witted and ignorant, they do not know whether milk is wholesome or unwholesome, they do not know the root source from which the illness arises, and they do not know which medicines to prescribe or avoid. Because they lack any such understanding, their turbid obstructions are great.
The text states:
"If I were to praise the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings would sink into suffering. This is precisely that meaning.

If they hear of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, they will immediately grow weary of birth-and-death and rejoice in nirvana; thus, their false calculations and attachments are destroyed. Therefore, the five turbidities do not obstruct the Lesser Vehicle. As the text says:
"When I was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and consoled me with Brahma-sounds"—this refers precisely to that meaning.

Regarding the four *siddhāntas* in relation to the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*): the eon and life-span correspond to the Worldly (*loka-vyavahāra*); sentient beings and views correspond to the Personal (*pudgala-vyavahāra*); and afflictions correspond to the Therapeutic (*prātipakṣika*). By employing these three *siddhāntas*, one eliminates the five corruptions; thereafter, one preaches for them the Great Ultimate Truth *Siddhānta* (*paramārtha-siddhānta*).

If we discuss cause and effect, there are two causes and three effects; for a single person, there are four dharmas occurring simultaneously: the two obstacles of retribution and the two obstacles of affliction, with karma situated between them. Sentient beings are a provisional construction formed by causes; life is a provisional construction of continuity; and the provisional construction of mutual dependence can likewise be understood.

Sentient beings (*sattva*) are conventional designations based on sensation (*vedanā*); the four [aggregates] are conventional designations based on phenomena (*dharma*). The designation "name" (*nāma*) applies to both. Afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) pertain to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); the remaining three [categories] pertain to both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*).
Life spans are short while kalpas are long; the remaining three [types of kalpas] span both the short and the long.
A kalpa is merely time, whereas life span involves the discussion of time in relation to dharmas.
Kalpas encompass both the internal and external, while life span exists only within the internal.
The three minor calamities harm humans but not other beings; the three major calamities harm beings but not humans.
Minor kalpas apply only to the human realm, whereas major kalpas extend throughout the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); as for life, it extends across the five destinies and the three realms (*tridhātu*).

The *kalpa* is the common turbidity (*saṃkleśa*), while the four [other turbidities] are each individual turbidities. The *antarakalpa* is the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpakaṣāya*); the great *mahākalpa* encompasses both turbid and non-turbid periods. From a lifespan of eighty thousand years down to ten years constitutes a small *antarakalpa*, and eighty such cycles constitute a great *mahākalpa*.
Question:
Since you have spoken of the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya), what are the five clarities?
Answer:

By analogy with the three poisons of the heterodox and the orthodox: the heterodox refers to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), while the orthodox refers to the five purities. Since other-worldly pure lands are free from the heterodox three poisons, the obstacles of the five turbidities are light; this principle may be understood as such, and so forth.
From the passage beginning with "If my disciples claim for themselves... onwards, this is the fourth section, which refutes the false and exhorts toward the true.

It states that if a disciple of the Buddha can personally believe and understand [the teaching], whereas one who does not believe and understand is neither a true disciple nor an Arhat; thus, it earnestly urges the assembly to believe, accept, and understand.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, distinguishing the true from the false; second, providing exemptions and resolving doubts.
The first part is further divided into two sections.
First, if one has neither heard nor understood [the teaching], one is not a true disciple.
Second, if one hears it but does not believe or accept it, one falls into the conceit of superiority (*adhimāna*).

Just as disciples of the world follow the teacher’s Dharma to succeed to and transmit the lamp of the teachings, if one has neither heard nor understood, there is no Dharma to follow; how, then, can such a person be called a disciple?

In the past, the Tathāgata taught the three vehicles by opening them up through the five turbidities; you followed these teachings and attained nirvāṇa, and because you have heard and understood them, you are called disciples.
Now that the five turbidities have been removed, I teach the One for you—why do you not hear it and why do you not understand it?
"Not hearing" refers to not hearing the teaching;
"not knowing" refers to not knowing the practice.
To be not true is to be not the principle; to be not a disciple is to be not a person.
Next, from "Furthermore, Śāriputra" onwards, the second section clarifies those who, lacking faith, have developed overweening pride (*adhimāna*); this serves to urge them toward faith.
Why? Because you claim for yourself that this is your final birth (*paścima-bhava*), yet even this body is still immeasurable; in truth, it is not your final birth.
"You claim for yourself that you have reached the ultimate goal, yet two hundred yojanas still remain; in truth, you have not reached the ultimate.
To claim what one has not attained as attained—is this not the pride of overestimation?"

A true Arhat, having eliminated turbidity and sharpened their faculties, knows that [their attainment] is not ultimate. Believing in the True Dharma and not yet being in their final body, they do not give rise to overweening pride; knowing it is not ultimate, they believe in the ultimate. Thus, believing in the oneness of principle constitutes the oneness of practice, free from overweening pride.

If one has faith, then one believes the Teaching; this constitutes the unity of the Teaching. If one is a disciple of the Buddha, then one is a person of the same kind as the Buddha—this constitutes the unity of the person.

Regarding the section "Except for after the Buddha’s extinction" and below, the second part opens an exception to resolve doubts: first, it provides the exception that after the Buddha’s extinction, one does not incur the offense of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Next, from "Why is this so?
Because the Buddha has passed away" onwards, it clarifies that good people are difficult to find and profound sutras are difficult to understand, yet one does not thereby fall into arrogance.
If the Buddha were still in the world and one did not believe or accept this sutra when it was being correctly preached, they would not be a true Arhat but would have become conceited;

however, if one attains Arhatship only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, yet clings exclusively to provisional sutras and does not believe in the perfect Dharma, such a person is permitted to be considered free from conceit.
Furthermore, although this sutra still exists even after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, if one does not believe in it or accept it, should this not be considered overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?

Such a person may immediately be cleared of this charge; for even though this sutra exists after the Buddha’s passing, those who can understand its words and meaning are difficult to encounter. Thus, it is permitted that even an Arhat might lack faith and understanding without this being considered overweening pride.
Next, the doubts are addressed:
If after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa it is difficult to encounter those who can interpret the sūtras, and if those who have attained arhatship enter parinirvāṇa forever, how is this explained?

It is explained that although such persons conceive the thought that they have entered extinction, after they pass away they are reborn in other lands beyond this realm; there they encounter other Buddhas, hear this sūtra, and immediately attain definitive realization.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary), fascicle 93, in its explanation of the "Chapter on Certainty" (*Niya-ta-pada*), states:
"If an Arhat receives a body from a previous life, that body must necessarily perish; dwelling in what place, then, could he fully realize the Buddha-way?"
Answer:

"The Arhat has exhausted the causes and conditions of the outflows within the three realms and will no longer be reborn therein. Beyond the three realms, there exists a pure Buddha-land where even the name of affliction does not exist; in that land, in the presence of the Buddha, they shall hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and fully realize the path to Buddhahood."
He then cited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, saying:

"If there are arhats who, not having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, claim for themselves that they have attained nirvāṇa, I shall proclaim this matter to them in other lands, saying: 'You shall all become Buddhas.'"
The *Śāstra* has already cited the sūtra as proof; now, in explaining the sūtra, we shall again rely on the *Śāstra* for interpretation.
Master Nanyue said:
"The 'other Buddhas' are the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*); when Arhats encounter them, they hear the sūtra and attain definitive understanding."

Furthermore, when Arhats cultivate the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha and see the Buddhas of the ten directions, they attain definitive understanding upon hearing these sutras preached for them.
Moreover, when ordinary practitioners repent with utmost sincerity and see the Buddhas of the ten directions preach for them, they likewise attain definitive understanding.
Master Yao said:

"A true Arhat must know for himself; [if one] aspires toward the Great [Vehicle], those of sharp faculties will know for themselves, while those of middling or inferior faculties must know by hearing—therefore, it is said they 'know through hearing.'"
How could it be possible that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one would not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
or having heard it, would not believe it, only to attain understanding upon meeting another Buddha?
If even ordinary beings during the Dharma-ending age can still believe it, how much more so the sages?
"Except for those after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Some say:
"Ordinary beings have not yet realized the characteristics of dharmas; their vision is unclear and their minds are not firmly established, which is why they are easily led to faith."

The Arhat has realized the characteristics of dharmas; what he perceives is clear and distinct, and his resolve is firm. When he suddenly hears a divergent teaching, he does not readily accept it, and thus it is said that he "does not believe. This meaning is necessarily so.
Therefore, Śāriputra said:
"Could it be that a māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb my mind?
According to this interpretation, it refers to an arhat and not to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), and so forth.
This is merely an alternative interpretation; this particular meaning is not adopted here.
From "Śāriputra" onwards is the fifth section, which clarifies that there is no falsehood in order to stop the slanderous minds of beings.
This consists of three parts:
first, the exhortation to believe that Śākyamuni has spoken the truth, as it says:
"You all should with one mind believe, understand, receive, and uphold the Buddha’s words."
Next, to encourage faith in all Buddhas, it is said:
"The words of all Buddhas are not false. Since the Way of all Buddhas is the same, one should further increase one's faith and acceptance.
The conclusion is subsequently established as not in vain; therefore, it is said:
"There is no other vehicle; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle.
The second verse consists of one hundred and twenty-one lines and is divided into two parts:
First, there are four lines and one phrase that versify the preceding promise to answer;
subsequently, there are one hundred and sixteen lines and three phrases that versify the actual answer.
Regarding the preceding promise to answer, there are three parts:
That is to say, there are two aspects: conforming to the admonition and the exclusion. Here, we do not recite the portion conforming to the admonition, but only the portion excluding and admonishing.
The exclusion of the assembly is twofold:
the first three and a half lines of verse recite the aforementioned retreat of the five thousand.
The next two lines praise the purity of the assembly mentioned above; the following line praises the exhortation to listen.

Arrogance (*adhimāna*) and pride (*māna*) leading to lack of faith are common to all four assemblies; however, among the two groups of renunciants who practice the Path and attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they falsely claim to have attained the fruits of sainthood—this gives rise specifically to arrogance; those who dwell in the secular world and boast of their own excellence mostly give rise to pride; and women, whose wisdom is shallow, frequently produce deviant views.

Regarding "not seeing one's own faults": when the three types of loss shroud the mind, concealing flaws and exalting virtues such that one cannot engage in self-reflection, this is a person devoid of shame; conversely, if one does see one's own faults, this is a monk possessed of modesty.

Regarding the phrase "having deficiencies and leaks in the precepts": a failure in the restraint (*saṃvara*) is called a "deficiency" (*chidra*); a failure in that which is concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata*) or the Path (*mārga-sahagata*) is called a "leak" (*srotas*). Because one lacks the Path and meditative concentration, evil thoughts arise within, like a jade containing internal flaws;
because one lacks the restraint, the body and speech move outwardly, like flaws exposed on the surface of jade.
Because one conceals these transgressions for oneself, it is called "guarding and cherishing."

"Those of small wisdom" do not possess the wisdom of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), but instead have mundane small wisdom; they falsely claim that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) to be without outflows (*anāsrava*). Because it is the smallest among the small, it is called "small wisdom."

Regarding the term "dregs and husks": because they lack the moisture of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), they are like dregs; because they lack the wisdom of principle (*yili*), they are like husks.

These five thousand people possessed mundane meditation like dregs and possessed literal understanding like husks; they were attached to the words and lost the underlying meaning, like husks without rice.

Furthermore, "dregs and chaff" is a metaphor for those who lack the great capacity; "branches and leaves" is a metaphor for those who are not excellent vessels. Since none of them are fit for employment, they must be sent away.
"Śāriputra, listen well" refers to the verse that reiterates the preceding injunction, commanding him to listen attentively.

From the line "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" onwards, there are one hundred and sixteen lines of three phrases; this constitutes the verse for the formal response to the preceding [questions], which is further divided into two parts.
First, from "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" downwards, there are seventy-three lines and one phrase, which constitute the verses for the four chapters on the Buddhas.
From the line "Now I am also like this" onwards, there are forty-three and a half lines of verse summarizing the preceding chapter on Śākyamuni.
This section is further divided into four parts;
first, from "That which all Buddhas have attained" onwards, there are thirty-four lines and three phrases summarizing the preceding chapter on the Buddhas.
From "Incalculable eons past" onwards, second, there are twenty-seven and a half lines in verse praising the gate of the Buddhas of the past;
from "The World-Honored Ones of future ages" onwards, third, there are six and a half lines in verse praising the gate of the Buddhas of the future;
from "Worshipped by devas and humans" onwards, fourth, there are four and a half lines in verse praising the gate of the Buddhas of the present.
Now, regarding the first verse within the section on the Buddhas, there are generally three differences between it and the prose commentary:
first, mutual absence; second, intermittent occurrence; and third, differing patterns of expansion and contraction.
In the preceding section, there was a praise of the rarity of the Dharma but no mention of the five turbidities; in this verse, there is a mention of the five turbidities but no praise of the Dharma.
Previously, the Dharma was praised first, followed by the clarification of its non-falsity, thereby opening up the provisional to reveal the real;
now, the opening up of the provisional to reveal the real comes first, followed by the clarification of its non-falsity.
In the preceding section, the exhortation to faith was explained in conjunction with non-falsity; now, the exhortation to faith is treated separately from non-falsity.

I personally maintain that in the preceding part, Śākyamuni’s skillful means were used to explain the provisional aspects of all Buddhas, whereas in the verses, Śākyamuni’s reality is used to explain how all Buddhas manifest the One—this constitutes the fourth difference.
This initial verse-text consists of five parts:
first, from "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" downward, five lines and three phrases, which eulogize the Buddhas' employment of skillful means;
second, from "I have established these expedients" downward, thirteen lines, which eulogize the Buddhas' revelation of the ultimate truth.
3. From "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha" below, for four and a half lines, there is a verse on the Chapter of the Buddhas exhorting faith;
4. From "If I surpass all sentient beings" below, for nine and a half long lines, there is a verse on the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*);
5. "I possess skillful means" below, for two lines, there is a verse on the aforementioned non-falsity.
Now, first, the explanation of the opening of the provisional (*upāya*). The text is divided into two parts:
first, four lines and one phrase of verse which praise the actual application of the provisional;
second, one and a half lines of verse which praise the intent behind applying the provisional.
Regarding the first point: "The dharma attained by all Buddhas" refers to attaining the various provisional dharmas through the cultivation of the path.
From "immeasurable power of skillful means" downward, the verse praises the aforementioned countless skillful means and the various causes and conditions used to expound all dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "the mental inclinations of sentient beings," this versifies the aforementioned teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Within the verse, the characteristics of such appropriateness are extensively set forth; that is to say, it illuminates the capacities of the nine dharma realms and expounds the seven expedient means. Since these nine and seven cannot be definitively fixed, they are described as "various" (*aneka*).
According to what is appropriate for desires, one should apply the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta*;
according to what is appropriate for dispositions, one should apply the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta*;
and according to what is appropriate for evil karma, one should apply the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.

The manifestation of aspiration is called "mindfulness" (*smṛti*); their diversity as dharma-gates is called "various" (*nānāvidha*); what was practiced in the past is called "nature" (*dhātu*); present delight is called "desire" (*chanda*). Alternatively, one may practice desire until it becomes a nature, and once a nature is established, it gives rise to the habitual desire for it, and so forth.
Regarding "good and evil karma," it is said that the seven stages of expedient means (saptavidha-upāya) are transmitted as good and evil, and so forth.

The Buddha, having illuminated the dispositions and inclinations of these various expedient means through his skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), subsequently employs various causes, conditions, and parables to preach the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*) according to what is appropriate for each, as well as the twelvefold canon (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), as explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Regarding the phrase "those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings," this one and a half lines conclude the intention behind the provisional application of skillful means.

Because their faculties were dull in previous lives and they lack the capacity now, they are unable to hear the Great [Vehicle], and thus it is said, "they do not practice the profound and wondrous Way.

Because they were attached to desires in previous lives with heavy obstructions and are now afflicted by manifold sufferings, they can only hear the inferior [teaching]; therefore, it is said, "for them, I preach Nirvana."
From the verse beginning "I say this is an expedient means" onwards is the second section, consisting of thirteen lines, which praises the manifestation of reality by all Buddhas.
This text is divided into four parts;
first, three lines praise the oneness of principle (*tattva-ekatva*).
"Causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom" summarizes the first of the great causal conditions.
"Decisively expounding the Mahāyāna" generally summarizes the opening, revealing, awakening to, and realizing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
“Entering the Mahāyāna as the foundation” praises the aforementioned entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

From “The sons of the Buddha, their minds pure” onwards, the second section consists of four and a half lines, praising the aforementioned point that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only Bodhisattvas, thereby clarifying the first aspect of the person (*pudgala*).
The commentary above states that these are bodhisattvas being transformed; the verses extensively demonstrate that all such people of various skillful means become true persons.

"There is a son of the Buddha whose mind is pure" refers specifically to those of the Separate Teaching (biejiao); for this son of the Buddha, the Mahāyāna sūtras are preached, and upon receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], his heart rejoices, whereby he becomes a truly realized person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).

Regarding the phrase "whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas": "śrāvakas" includes those who have also attained the stage of pratyekabuddhas; "bodhisattvas" includes those who have also attained the six perfections, the general teachings, and so forth, as well as all other bodhisattvas.
The phrase "all shall undoubtedly attain Buddhahood" refers to the seven kinds of skillful means, wherein there are none who are not sons of the Buddha; this constitutes the first verse-line.

From the line "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions" onwards is the third section, consisting of one line and three phrases, which praises how the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings using only the Single Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna), without any other vehicles, whether two or three.
If the Buddhas of the ten directions teach only a single Dharma, this is the teaching of oneness;
the use of provisional names to guide beings is the teaching of skillful means.
By restating the three provisional teachings to reveal the Buddha’s wisdom as the one teaching, the meaning of the text becomes clear.
"There is no other vehicle" means there is nothing remaining beyond the complete entry into the distinct teaching.
"Non-dual" means there is no duality of the partial and the full as contrasted within the universal teaching.
"Absence of three" means the absence of the three [vehicles] within the Tripitaka.
Such pairs and triads are all provisional names used to guide sentient beings; now there is only the single Buddha’s Perfect Teaching Vehicle.

From the verse "The Buddhas appear in the world; this alone is the one true reality" onwards, the fourth section consists of three lines and three phrases. This verse summarizes the preceding passage, "Whatever they do, it is always for one purpose," which constitutes the first textual unit.

The "matter" is itself the practice; the statement, “one never uses the Lesser Vehicle to deliver sentient beings,” is a verse summarizing the meaning of the aforementioned constant pursuit of the one great matter.

"The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna and thereby delivers sentient beings" praises the preceding point that he uses only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to instruct and awaken sentient beings.
The subsequent line explains the intention of not delivering them by means of the Hīnayāna.

From the verse beginning "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha" onwards, the third section consists of four and a half lines; this verse summarizes the preceding exhortation to have faith, as it was said above: "You all should believe what the Buddha has spoken."
There are two parts within the verse:
first, two and a half lines which exhort faith by citing the fruit; second, the two lines beginning with "Śāriputra," which exhort faith by citing the cause.

Within the section on citing the fruits, the first one and a half lines cite the internal mind: "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, who is non-deceptive. This clarifies that the Buddha’s mind is pure; because he has already severed the defilements of ignorance, stinginess, and all evils, he speaks from within a pure mind, and is therefore trustworthy.
The line "I adorn my body with marks" clarifies external form (*rūpa*).

When the physical characteristics of the body are brilliant and radiant, and the complexion is dignified and majestic—such that there is no darkness or delusion within and radiance shines forth without—one will not deceive others with one's speech and will be honored by the multitude; thus, when one proclaims the seal of the Mahāyāna, it shall be trusted and accepted.
The two lines beginning with "I originally established a vow" constitute the exhortation to believe by citing the cause; this is further divided into two parts:
first, the line beginning with "I originally established a vow" cites the former vow;
second, the line beginning with "As I formerly [vowed]" clarifies the fulfillment of that vow.

In the past, my vow was not merely a personal pledge for enlightenment, but also a pledge that all sentient beings should enter together into the Buddha-wisdom. Now, in order to fulfill that vow, I speak; this is indeed worthy of belief. Since enlightenment is now perfected and sentient beings have likewise entered [the path], and since you yourself have realized the Buddha-wisdom, you can verify that my vow was not in vain. This concludes the section on citing causes to encourage faith.
Question:
Since your original vow is universal, yet sentient beings remain so numerous, how can your vow be fulfilled?
Answer:
The Buddhas benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; here, the present [verse] clarifies that their vows are fulfilled in the current age.

The section beginning with "If I encounter sentient beings" constitutes the fourth part, consisting of nine and a half lines. It enumerates the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Previously, the five corruptions were explained in the chapter on Śākyamuni; now, they appear at the end of the general section on the Buddhas and are further reiterated within the specific section on Śākyamuni. This demonstrates that all Buddhas emerge together amidst the five corruptions, each first employing the *triyāna* and subsequently the *ekayāna*.
This text consists of four parts:
first, one line, which generally explains how the five turbidities obstruct the Great [Vehicle];
second, six lines, which specifically explain how the five turbidities obstruct the Three [Vehicles].
3. One line clarifies that the teaching of the Small Vehicle is a skillful means employed for the sake of the five corruptions;
4. One and a half lines clarify that the teaching of the Small Vehicle is for the sake of the Great [Vehicle], whereby the small [vehicle] remedies the five corruptions and the great vow may arise.
Regarding the phrase "If I encounter sentient beings," the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 12, states:

"At the beginning of the kalpa, beings descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to this world; there were no distinctions of male or female, nor of honor or lowliness. Because they arose together in the world as a multitude, they are called 'sentient beings' (*sattva*)."
This refers to the very beginning.
If one takes up the various aggregates (skandhas) and applies the provisional designation "sentient being," this refers to the reception of retribution throughout a single lifetime.
If it is said that they are called "sentient beings" because they undergo birth in various places, this refers to the circulation through the five destinies by the power of karma.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"There are ten kinds of sentient beings, namely: long, short, square, round, triangular, blue, yellow, red, white, and purple."
How is it that the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings is so long?
While in the hells, they undergo inconceivable suffering with their bodies and harbor immeasurable and boundless evil thoughts in their minds;
while among animals, they prey upon one another with their bodies and torment one another with their minds.
When they were among the hungry ghosts, their bodies were like burning mountains and their minds like boiling cauldrons; their false views were rampant, and they were obstinate, deluded, and fierce.

When they were among humans, their body, speech, and mind constantly performed unbeneficial acts, bringing themselves toil and hardship; their body, speech, and mind constantly dwelt on unbeneficial matters, binding and entangling themselves.
When they were among the gods, they were addicted to and defiled by the six sense objects, indulging in wanton play and sport; they did not hear the True Dharma and blocked the source of merit.
This is called the long duration of birth and death for sentient beings.
What is the short duration of birth and death for sentient beings?
While in the hells, if one can, in a single thought-moment, take up the precepts with a tranquil mind;
When in the realm of animals, one can for a single thought-moment settle the mind in stillness and take refuge in the Triple Gem;
when in the realm of hungry ghosts, one can for a single thought-moment settle the mind in stillness and quiet the sense faculties;
when among humans, one can cultivate the six perfections, support one's parents, revere the Triple Gem, and adorn the body, speech, and mind with goodness.
While in the heavens, one abandons celestial pleasures for the joy of observing the precepts, practicing dhyāna, teaching and reciting, and maintaining pure conduct with few words;
this is what is meant by the shortness of the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings. What, then, is the long duration of the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings?

Just as in Uttarakuru, where there is no sense of "mine" regarding any object, and upon casting off the body one inevitably ascends to heaven, from heaven ascending further to heaven, moving only toward higher realms of goodness—this is called the square and rectangular nature of birth and death.
What is meant by the "circular" cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) for sentient beings?
It refers solely to their revolving within the three miserable realms and the four destinies, turning in a complete circle like a whirling torch or a circling smoke—this is it.
What is meant by the "triangular" cycle of birth and death?
This refers to wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, the indeterminate, and so forth.
What is meant by sentient beings having a "blue" cycle of birth and death?
It is this state of constantly entering the dark hells and being perpetually terrified.
What is the yellow death-and-rebirth of sentient beings?
It is the withered yellowness of hungry ghosts who are emaciated by hunger.
What is the red death-and-rebirth of sentient beings?
As for animals devouring one another, with blood flowing so as to be brilliant—this is what it refers to.
What is meant by "the white [karma] of sentient beings in birth and death"?
It refers to the white karma of the wholesome paths among humans and devas; for example, when various devas are approaching death, other devas say to them:
"Go, you who have been born into the human realm.
When a person is approaching death, their kinsmen and friends say to them:
"Go toward the heavenly realms."
"One should know that these two places are the white [realm] of birth and death.
Furthermore, the fifth [section] says:
"The mind paints hell as black, the hungry ghosts as pigeon-colored, animals as yellow, humans as red, and devas as white. What is the meaning of this?"
Answer: "The previous passage spoke of the retributions of the five destinies; the present passage speaks of the karma created within the five destinies; thus, they differ, and so forth.

Regarding such sentient beings, if they are to encounter the Buddhas: sentient beings are scorched by their own suffering and affliction, while the Buddhas rescue all things through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); because compassion and suffering are opposites, it is said that they "encounter" one another.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s suchness is identical to the suchness of sentient beings; it is a single suchness without a second suchness. Because their natures are interrelated, they are said to "meet.

Now, Great Compassion constantly takes pity on sentient beings; yet if one were to instruct them according to the ways of humans and devas, they would fall into darkness and delusion, merely escaping the cycle of birth and death characterized by blue, yellow, red, purple, square, round, angular, or pointed forms, rather than being taught the Buddha-way.

If I encounter sentient beings and cause them to practice only the Hinayana, I would fall into stinginess and greed; this is unacceptable, as it results in only escaping the twenty-five realms of existence.
If I encounter sentient beings and instruct them only in the general or specific [teachings], I would fall into partiality and lose the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Now, I cause all sentient beings to attain the wondrous wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), so that they may realize that everything is the Buddha-dharma and nothing is not the Right Path; this is to teach them entirely by means of the Buddha-way, whereby the suffering of birth and death is forever exhausted.
I have always spoken thus: it is only because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and their transgressions are heavy that they cannot fulfill their wishes.

In the past, there was a Buddha named Dwelling in Non-dwelling, who made a vow that the sentient beings of his own land would all attain Buddhahood on the same day and at the same time, and enter parinirvāṇa on that very day.

Furthermore, prior to the Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Samatā, who also made the vow that the beings in his own land and throughout the ten directions would likewise attain Buddhahood on the same day and enter parinirvāṇa on that very same day.
"There is a Buddha today; what, then, of sentient beings?
The Buddha said: "Stop!"
"Stop!
What I said previously was merely that one has obtained a human body.
Is it possible to make a vow to cause those in the five realms of existence to attain Buddhahood on the same day?
The Buddha said:

"One cannot achieve the Unsurpassed Way with a body that is not a fit vessel; one must first transform those in the three evil realms so they may attain human or celestial rebirth, and only then can one fulfill this wish."
"How can those in the three miserable destinies, which are not wholesome paths, achieve Buddhahood?
It is like a person seeking a hoard of jewels who would not seek them in the air.
From the phrase "I know these sentient beings" onwards, the second section consists of six lines, specifically clarifying the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*) in five parts:
First, the second line clarifies the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
"Roots of goodness" refers to the true nature of reality (*tathatā-satyalakṣaṇa*); because one does not rely on these roots of goodness, one does not bring about greatness.
"Being firmly attached to the five desires" is the very root of all evils.
From delusion (*moha*) and craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), my illness arises.
From the line "From the subtle form conceived in the womb" onwards is the second section; one line specifically clarifies the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the arising of a single thought-moment constitutes the karma for future action; this karma is the embryo. Since embryonic karma is inexhaustible, it continues uninterrupted from lifetime to lifetime; this lack of interruption is precisely what constitutes growth.

The subtle form at the moment of conception consists of the five aggregates (*skandha*). These aggregates are called "the world" (*loka*); as the life-force maintains these aggregates and brings them into the world, beginning from the stage of the thin curd (*kalala*) until old age and death, it is termed "growing from life to life," which constitutes the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
The *Śrī-āśraya-śarīra-sūtra* states:
"When an ordinary person receives a body, during the first seven days it has not yet undergone transformation; in the second seven days there is the appearance of birth, like thin curd;
in the third seven days it is like thick curd; in the fourth seven days it is like solidified butter; in the fifth seven days it is like unbaked clay; in the sixth seven days..."
Like a mass of flesh, from that mass of flesh five blisters arise after seven times seven [fortnights]: the head, hands, and feet;
then another five blisters after eight times seven: one head, two shoulders, and two wrists; then twenty-four blisters continue to arise after nine times seven:
four blisters form the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, while twenty blisters become the two [hands].
The ten fingers undergo seventeen transformations to manifest the appearance of the abdomen;
gradually, the skin and bones separate to form various distinct features, giving rise to seven hundred sinews and seven thousand vessels. Each required feature is then colored by a specific wind:
the white wind colors those requiring a white appearance, and so on for the other winds as well; because of the fragrant wind, one remains secure and at ease.
If one is upright but lacks peace and stability due to foul odors, one will become ugly, deformed, and perverse;
later, upon emerging from the womb and consuming the five grains, eighty thousand species of worms will arise within.
"Entering the dense forest of false views" and below constitutes the third section, a single line, which refers to the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

The five views are intermingled like a thick and luxuriant forest: if one exists, it is the view of eternalism; if one does not exist, it is the view of annihilationism. From these two views, sixty-two [views] arise. Alternatively, it is said that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) calculate the self (*ātman*) through four propositions:

"form is the self," "the self is apart from form," "form is large and the self is small with the self dwelling within form," and "the self is large and form is small with form dwelling within the self. These four propositions apply likewise to each of the other four aggregates (*skandha*), making twenty in total.
The three periods [of time] constitute sixty, and together with the fundamental [period], they form sixty-two, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Next, from "Deeply attached to the false" onwards, the fourth section consists of one verse which describes the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), as per the text.

From "In thousands of millions of billions" onwards is the fifth section, one line, which eulogizes the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the age). The absence of the Buddha-dharma for a long duration constitutes the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
Furthermore, because the aforementioned four defilements (*kaṣāya*) are concentrated within this period, it is named the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.

Regarding the phrase "such persons are difficult to save": because they are obstructed by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), they do not believe in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and thus cannot be saved.

As for those who rely on conceptual understanding (*vikalpa*), their every thought-moment consists of evil perceptions; since they lack the self-awareness of right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), they do not see the Buddha. Because their minds lack the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*), they do not hear the Dharma. Such a mind is difficult to save.
"Thus, Śāriputra," and so forth, is the third section, one line, which provisionally teaches the Small Vehicle as the text describes.

"Although I speak of nirvāṇa," and so forth, is the fourth section, one and a half lines, which ultimately causes entry into the Great Vehicle: by analyzing away the delusions of the three realms until they are exhausted, the cessation of form and the grasping for emptiness is not true cessation; rather, if one realizes through essence that ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and eternally quiescent, this is true cessation.

Although fundamental non-arising is quiescent, if one does not cultivate the Way, there is no means by which to realize it; therefore, it is said: "When the Buddha-sons have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in a future life."
From "I possess the power of skillful means" onwards is the fifth section, consisting of two lines, which praises what was stated above:
that "you all should believe that what the Buddha has spoken is not false."
The exhortation to believe has already been concluded with the preceding verses; it is not in vain that they are now recited again.
The first two lines clarify that Śākyamuni first revealed the three [vehicles];
the subsequent two lines clarify that all Buddhas later manifest the reality (dharmatā), appearing alternately.
The final line clearly explains that [the teaching] is not in vain; since the former was provisional and the latter is the reality, these truthful words are indeed not false—do not harbor doubts.

From "In the past, incalculable kalpas ago" onwards, the second section, spanning twenty-seven and a half lines, versifies the preceding chapter on the Buddhas of the Past. This text is divided into two parts:
the first two lines versify the opening of the three [vehicles], as found in the prose.

From "These World-Honored Ones" below, the second section consists of twenty-five and a half lines of verse. One [aspect] is revealed through these verses, while the preceding prose revealed the reality; together, they comprise four types of "one," which are now fully versified.
Within this, there are further two parts:
the first line briefly summarizes the three preceding [verses], all of which expound the One Vehicle Dharma; this constitutes the summary of the "One of Teaching.
"Transforming immeasurable sentient beings" constitutes the summary of the "One of Persons."
"Causing them to enter the Buddha-way" corresponds to the verse on the unity of principle (*li-yi*), while simultaneously attaining the unity of practice (*xing-yi*).

Next, from "Furthermore, all the Great Holy Lords" onwards, the second section consists of twenty-four and a half lines, which extensively versify the manifestation of unity by way of the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*).
Regarding the text, there are two parts.

The first one and a half lines provide a general summary based on the five vehicles to manifest the oneness [of the Buddha]. "The multitudes of devas and human beings" cites the various vehicles to clarify the oneness of persons;
"further employing diverse skillful means" cites the various practices to manifest the oneness of practice, while simultaneously attaining the oneness of teaching.
The primary meaning (*paramārtha*) is precisely the oneness of principle.

Regarding the phrase "different expedient means" (*anya-upāya*) and below: the Buddha-nature as the true cause is the primary meaning of principle; if one employs the perfect and wondrous right contemplation, this is the expedient of the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and is not called "different.
If one employs the seven expedient contemplations to assist in manifesting the primary meaning, these are called "different expedient means."

Next, from "If there are sentient beings" onwards, the second section consists of twenty-three lines, which specifically distinguishes the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*) to reveal the ultimate truth; this is divided into three parts:
first, two lines that open the Bodhisattva vehicle;
next, the second part, one line that opens the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Third, twenty lines open the way for the vehicle of devas and humans.
First, the two lines beginning with "If there are any classes of sentient beings" open the way for the bodhisattva vehicle.
If explained according to the five vehicles, it refers solely to the Bodhisattva vehicle of the six perfections;
if explained according to the seven expedient means, it also encompasses both the general and specific Bodhisattva vehicles.
Why is this? Although those of the three vehicles and the Mahāyāna all practice the six perfections, there is a difference in how they direct their minds.
One who practices the six perfections with a mind of grasping at characteristics is a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka.
The signless (*animitta*) corresponds to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śikṣā*);
the sequential practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) through non-characteristic and signlessness corresponds to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śikṣā*).
Here, only the six perfections are listed; it is not yet known which teaching they definitively belong to.

Referring back to the previous passage which states, "Furthermore, by means of other skillful expedients," this does not refer solely to the bodhisattvas of the six perfections; rather, it refers to the expedient means of the bodhisattvas of the three teachings.

Those who formerly heard the Dharma have all already achieved the unity of teaching; those who formerly practiced the six perfections have all already achieved the unity of practice; likewise, these various individuals have all already achieved the unity of person, have all already achieved the Buddha-way, and have all already achieved the unity of principle.
From the line, "After the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, if there is a person with a virtuous and gentle mind," it is revealed that both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the One Vehicle.
How is this known?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* praises the mind of an arhat as being well-tamed and supple; furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Abiding in a tamed mind is the practice of the noble ones. It is from these sources that we know this.
"In the past, those with virtuous and gentle minds all achieved the One Practice; that all such people are 'One' refers to the person; that they attain the Buddha-way is the 'One Principle.
Regarding 'Making Offerings to the Śarīra,' this is the third section, consisting of twenty lines, which opens the way for the vehicles of humans and devas."

This does not clarify the vehicles of humans and devas, but merely explains the construction of images and stupas, as well as single-mindedness versus distraction; thus, one knows these are the karmic activities of humans and devas.
The Master Di (Dilun) interprets it, saying:
"The 'Child' refers to the stage of the Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*), which is free from the dualistic desires of the two vehicles and ordinary beings."
"To pile sand into a stupa—sand is non-attachment, while the stupa is the accumulation of various practices, containing within it the mind of perfect enlightenment.

That [previous] view held that understanding the meaning through non-arising constitutes profound penetration; now, however, it is said that this deviates from the text and is narrow-minded in its interpretation.
Why is this? One who has ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) should naturally attain Buddhahood; how could this be considered remarkable, like an asura crossing the ocean?

Now, using the play of children with sand and the singing of a distracted mind, one points to the subtle and immediately adheres to it—this is as inconceivable as an ordinary person crossing the ocean. The Buddha clearly and extensively harmonized the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), ensuring not even the slightest merit was omitted; yet you discard this broad intention of gathering all beings and take directly to the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
If it were as explained above, it would hardly encompass even those of the Two Vehicles, let alone ordinary worldlings.
While the profundity of the treatise is indeed consistent with the sūtra, its extensive definition deviates from the scriptural text.
Question:
The minor virtues of humans and devas should result in karmic retribution; why, then, is it said that they have all already attained the Buddha-way?
Answer:

This should clarify the meaning of the three Buddha-natures. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, there is a Buddha-nature that those with roots of goodness possess, while those who are icchantikas lack; this refers precisely to the minor virtues of humans and devas."

Bowing the head and raising the hand is like beginning a mountain with a single basket of earth or initiating a tree of girth as thick as two arms with a single hair; what was previously called "abiding in retribution" before the skillful means were revealed is now, through the opening of skillful means, the "enabling cause" (緣因) of Buddha-nature, which is capable of leading toward Bodhi and realizing the meaning of manifesting the ultimate truth.
This consists of two parts:
the first nineteen lines clarify the reality by means of the seeds of the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) formed through the minor virtues of devas and humans;
the final line clarifies the reality by means of the seeds of the revealing cause (*jñāna-hetu*). These can be understood by following the text.
The first nineteen lines constitute ten sections:

the first three and a half lines concern the Deva-yāna (the Vehicle of the Gods) in relation to the construction of stupas. Because one gives away wealth and treasures with a sincere mind when the causal conditions arise, one spontaneously and naturally experiences bliss at the time of the result; therefore, this is the Deva-yāna.
Regarding "wooden *kai*": there is a wood named *kai* in Chang’an that is also suitable for making images.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"If one places even as much as a mustard seed or a grain of millet of the Buddha’s *śarīra* within a small stupa, the Heaven of the Thirty-three will naturally receive its karmic retribution."
This is precisely that meaning.

Next, from "even down to children" onwards, is the second section, consisting of one line. A child playing in the sand to build a stupa is a human action (*puruṣakāra*); because at the time of the cause one performs good deeds with a carefree and easygoing mind, whereas at the time of the fruit one exerts effort with deliberate intent to seek happiness, it is therefore a human action.
Next, from "If a person, for the sake of the Buddha... onwards is the third section. These four lines clarify the meritorious karma of creating images with a sincere mind.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* does not permit the use of glue, as doing so incurs the offense of a transgression of resolve (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding the use of this sutra, ancient masters said:
"In foreign lands, it is used as tree resin.
Guangzhai stated:
"In some places, it is strictly necessary to use glue made from ox-hide when using images; however, if other materials are available, one must not use it.
Some say: "The juice of large beans may serve as a substitute for the glue-water."
"However, cowhide is ultimately an impure substance and will result in an impure karmic retribution later on.
Impure money is unfit for making images; one should exchange it for pure money in accordance with the Dharma to create an image."

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* does not permit the use of arsenic or foul-smelling substances; the *Śīlasūtra* does not allow the creation of half-body images, for doing so incurs the offense of "loss of intention," whereby wholesome signs do not arise and one falls back into the cycle of birth and death.

However, each type of image has its own intended representation: a Buddha for the main hall must be seated; a Buddha of the "transmission" (or "informal") style may be either seated or reclining; and a Buddha of the "active" or "processional" style must be standing.
Furthermore, a disciple must not sit before an image established in a stupa or hall, because this place definitively belongs to the Buddha;
however, if one is in a layperson’s house, one may sit elsewhere, though one cannot remain standing for long before the image—if one requests permission to sit, it is permissible.
Yet, one must never sit before an image that is intended to be stood before, and so forth.
Next, from "even down to children" onwards is the fourth section, one line, which clarifies human karma.
Next, from "such people as these" onwards is the fifth section, one and a half lines, which concludes by manifesting the reality.

All people are originally one person; as they gradually accumulate merit and fulfill the mind of great compassion, they immediately achieve the oneness of practice. The Buddha-way is the oneness of principle. Having already attained Buddhahood, they are further able to manifest the fourfold oneness, yet they transform only Bodhisattvas—this is what is meant by the "oneness of teaching," and so forth.

Next, from "If a person [makes offerings] at a stūpa or temple" onwards, the sixth section consists of three and a half lines concerning the meritorious karma of making offerings with various sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
As for "copper gong" (*tóngbō*), people in Chang'an called the *lùpán* (the pinnacle ornament) a "copper gong"; since he was translating scriptures there, he used that local name.
Next, from "If a person with a distracted mind" onwards is the seventh section; this single line clarifies the karma of making offerings with sensory objects using a distracted mind.
Next, from "Or there may be someone who prostrates" onwards is the eighth section; this single line clarifies the karma of making offerings to celestial beings through physical action.

Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground for a single phrase is the superior form of worship, which is the karma of devas; joining the palms and bowing the head is the intermediate form of worship, which is the karma of humans.
Next, from "With this offering... onwards, the ninth section consists of one and a half lines, which serves as the conclusion.

It is not only that [the teaching] reveals the reality and enables one to personally attain the Buddha-way, but it can also open up the provisional [teachings] and lead to *nirvāṇa* when the firewood is exhausted, and so forth.

Next, from "If a person scatters [flowers]" onwards, the tenth section consists of one line; this concerns verbal karma (*vāk-karman*). By analogy with what precedes, it should include the karmas of gods and humans, yet here only human karma is mentioned, and so forth.
"Namo" has great significance; some say:
"Deliver me, deliver me! You may bestow [merit] upon sentient beings.
If the Buddha replies:
The interpretation that "the Buddhas have delivered me" is not tenable.
The *Pañcaśīla Sūtra* speaks of "trembling with fear"; such trembling is precisely what one should offer to the Buddha.

The perils of birth and death are truly terrifying; since they cannot be rescued by the Great [Vehicle], we now follow the example of the Buddhas to deliver them through the Small [Vehicle]. It is therefore appropriate to offer these terrors to the Buddha, which is why the text says:
"Joyfully reciting 'Namo Buddha'."
"Joy" refers to the joy of attaining the ritual for saving sentient beings.
The *Pañcaśīla Sūtra* further states:
"Taking refuge means to bestow everything upon all sentient beings."

When Devadatta was at the point of death, he uttered "Namo. Before he could utter the word "Buddha," he fell into hell. The Buddha prophesied that after emerging from hell, he would become a Pratyekabuddha named Namo.
In foreign lands, those who worship images of deities made the heads of these images out of gold; when bandits came to steal them, they were unable to take them and cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! (Homage to the Buddha!)
He then obtained the head.

The next day, the assembly gathered and said, "If the celestial image has lost its head, it means there is no deity who comes to wear it; if there were one who wore it, how could it have lost its head?"
A deity immediately descended as a person and said:
"When the bandits come to take your head, you should immediately cry out:
'Namo Buddhāya!'"
"All the devas were thus startled and agitated; for this reason, they found an opportunity against me, and for this reason, they lost their heads.
The multitude asked, "Is the deva not superior to the Buddha?"
"If you are already not as good as them, why do you not now serve the Buddha?
The bandit replied, "If even one who merely utters 'Namo Buddha' can attain a heavenly rebirth, how much more so for a worthy person like you who utters 'Namo Buddha'?"
The honored deities of the ten directions dare not oppose it; simply practice with diligence and do not be indolent.
The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* states:
"If a person, at the moment of death, recites 'Namo Buddha,' they shall escape the hells."
How is this so?
It is like a person holding a single stone and placing it in water; the stone will surely sink without doubt. Yet, if one can place a hundred stones upon a boat, they will certainly not sink.
If one dies in this ordinary manner, one will inevitably enter the hells, like a stone placed in water;
however, if at the point of death one recites "Namo Buddha," the power of the Buddha causes one not to enter the hells, just as the power of a boat prevents a stone from sinking, and so forth.
The *Garbha-sūtra* and the *Kṣāntivādī-sūtra* state:

"Regarding those ninety-two billion people at the third great assembly in the Flower Grove Garden, they are those who, within the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, attained the vision of Maitreya by uttering 'Namo Buddha' even once."

Next, from "In all past Buddhas" onwards is the second section, which consists of one line clarifying the seeds of the cause. Following the previous pattern, there are the five types of seeds for the five vehicles—namely, those with signs, those without signs, those that are neither with nor without signs, those of the concentrated mind, and those of the distracted mind—and now all these are opened up and subsumed within the One Reality, and so forth.
"To hear even a single phrase with a sincere mind is the karma of a deva; to hear even a single phrase with a distracted mind is the karma of a human," and so forth.
Question:
For what reason is the Dharma-gate of the past Buddhas used to extensively clarify the Five Vehicles?
Answer:

The Buddhas of the three periods all employ the provisional to reveal the ultimate; however, because the future has not yet arisen and the present has only just begun its activity, their capacity for realization is weak.

The Buddhas of the past have long since employed the provisional, and those who have received their transformation have all attained the fourfold unity. Furthermore, they have extensively applied the provisional and revealed the ultimate throughout the ten directions; thus, their capacity for realization is powerful in practice.
Constructing arguments with empty words is not as good as verifying them through reality; therefore, regarding the Buddhas of the past, he extensively expounds upon the Five Vehicles.
From the line "The future World-Honored Ones" onwards, the third section consists of six and a half lines, which versify the chapter on the Buddhas of the future.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first one and a half lines versify the opening of the three;
the subsequent five lines versify the manifestation of the one.
"Delivering all sentient beings" constitutes one practice; this verse praises the first practice.

"The original vows of all Buddhas" constitutes one practice; this verse praises the first practice. Since the path practiced by the Buddhas is vowed to be made available so that others may attain it, is this not indeed the first practice?
The two lines concerning "the Buddhas of future ages" constitute one verse of instruction.

Regarding the phrase "knowing that dharmas are eternally without nature": the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is eternally abiding and lacks self-nature; it even lacks the nature of being causeless. That there is no nature, and even that this absence of nature is itself without nature—this is called "being without nature."

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha-seed arises from conditions": the Middle Way of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) is itself the Buddha-seed. For those who are deluded regarding this principle, sentient beings arise with ignorance as the condition;

for those who understand this principle, perfect enlightenment arises with teaching and practice as the conditions. To give rise to the Buddha-seed, one requires the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); this is the verse concerning the "One [Vehicle] of Teaching."
Furthermore, that which is "without nature" (wu-xing) is precisely the Buddha-nature as the true cause (zheng-yin fo-xing).
That "the seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions" refers to the conditional and the developmental (yuan-liao) natures.
Because the conditional nature assists the developmental nature, the true seed is able to arise; when one arises, all arise. These three natures are what is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

The single line, "This dharma abides in the station of dharmas," expresses a single principle: sentient beings and perfect enlightenment are of one suchness and not two; all do not transcend suchness, for all take suchness as their station.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding": the supramundane perfect enlightenment takes Suchness as its locus and also takes Suchness as its characteristic; since both locus and characteristic are eternally abiding, how could it not be so?
Mundane sentient beings likewise take Suchness as their locus and take Suchness as their characteristic; how, then, could they not be eternally abiding?
Since the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, are they not, indeed, of a single principle?
Furthermore, what is called the "world" refers to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas).
That which is "eternally abiding" is precisely the True Cause (zhengyin).

However, this primary cause (pradhāna-hetu) is not identical to the six dharmas, yet the conditions (pratyaya) and the enabling causes (hetu) are not separate from them. Because the primary cause is eternal, the conditions and enabling causes are also eternal; therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding."

"Having realized it at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)"—this citation of the fruit establishes the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real. At the site of enlightenment, this principle was already luminously pervasive; however, because the obstacles of sentient beings' minds were heavy, the expedient means of the three [vehicles] were provisionally bestowed, and so forth.

From "Worshipped by devas and humans" onwards, the fourth section consists of four and a half lines, which are verses on the chapter concerning the present Buddhas. Of the four sections in the preceding prose, three are now versified, while the final concluding section is not.
The first one and a half lines of verse express the intent of the transformation, specifically for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings.

The subsequent line, beginning with "knowing the foremost quiescence," praises the manifestation of reality mentioned above: "knowing the foremost quiescence" praises the oneness of principle (*li-yi*); "its reality is the Buddha-vehicle" either praises the oneness of teaching (*jiao-yi*) or the oneness of practice (*xing-yi*).
The following two lines, beginning with "Knowing the various practices of sentient beings," eulogize the revelation of the provisional (kaiquan), as per the text.

From "Now I am also like this" onwards, the second section consists of forty-three and a half lines, eulogizing the chapter on Śākyamuni; whereas the preceding prose lacks praise for the rarity of the Dharma, the verse includes all six aspects.

However, in the old commentary on the *Gāthā*, the original analogies were highlighted while the preceding and following texts were intermingled; thus, consulting the sub-commentary causes the eyes to spin, and hearing it explained causes the mind to become disordered, leading those of dull faculties into confusion.
I have previously composed and set forth the preceding [text], and now append this further commentary to the text so that it may serve as a mirror for myself.
However, the verses in the chapter on Śākyamuni generally contain two intentions:
the first praises what precedes, and the second follows from what comes below.

Those of superior faculties have already attained awakening, while those of middling faculties have not yet understood; therefore, it is necessary to employ analogies to correspond to the aforementioned teachings. Since an analogy does not arise in isolation but follows a specific cause, it is called the "basis of the analogy" (*pūrvapada*).

The *Kou* (Oral Tradition) formerly provided five analogies: first, the analogy of the elder; second, the analogy of seeking salvation; third, the analogy of expedient inducement; fourth, the analogy of equality; and fifth, the analogy of non-falsity.

However, the opening [analogy] is a general illustration and does not refer exclusively to the elder; it merely uses the thought of rescuing as a metaphor for saving one's children. Because it only partially illustrates the analogy of the fire, it was not employed [here].
Master Yao said:

"In the 'Expedient Means' chapter, from the passage 'The Buddhas teach according to what is appropriate' through the end of the prose section, the true reality of the One Vehicle is correctly revealed."
There are four chapters in total:
first, opening up the former "four threes" to establish the present "four ones";
second, because of the five turbidities, the One Vehicle cannot be taught;
Third, from "If my disciples claim for themselves... onwards, it clarifies those who do not attain [the fruit];
fourth, from "You should with single-mindedness believe and understand... onwards, it clarifies that [the teaching] is not false.
Although the beginning and end differ in their phrasing, when sought through the underlying intent, both are true.
The section on descending from the burning house is merely an illustration of the three chapters within the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) chapter:
from "For example" down to "I pray you will grant them at the proper time," constitutes the first illustration, the chapter on the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya).
From "He gave each of his sons an equal great carriage" up to "attaining what they had never experienced before," this is the second simile, the Chapter on Reality;
from "This elder gave these [carriages] equally to his sons" up to "how could there be any falsehood? this is the third simile, the Chapter on Non-falsity.
Master Xuanchang spoke of six analogies:
"First, the signs of the various calamities within the house;
second, that it is only the Awakened One who gives rise to the thought of the One Vehicle."
Third, for sentient beings who do not accept [the teaching], one speaks of matters that inspire fear;
fourth, one speaks of the bliss of the three vehicles.
Fifth, returning to explain the teaching of the One Vehicle;
sixth, concluding that [the teaching] is not false.
The Dragon Master spoke six parables:
"First, the house and the father and son illustrate how the Buddha rules the triple world to transform sentient beings;
second, the elder seeing the fire illustrates how I, with the Buddha-eye, observe the sentient beings within the six realms."
Third, the elder’s extinguishing of the fire is a metaphor for the Buddha’s three-week period when he was unable to deliver sentient beings because he could not employ the Great [Vehicle];
